messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Sorry to resurface this topic, but I am having similar complications with my analysis and would appreciate any input.

I have 17 sites that have multiple observations at each (less than 6 observations though), when I use the growth() function I get the error as mentioned above. However, when I try to model a multigroup SEM using the group() command in sem(), I get the following error:

Error in lav_samplestats_icov(COV = cov[[g]], ridge = ridge, x.idx = x.idx[[g]],  :  lavaan ERROR: sample covariance matrix is not positive-definite

I did not have this error before including the group() command in the code. Any thoughts for why this might be? Or any suggestions for how to control for repeated measurements at a site?

Thanks in advance for any help!

Code without group() that ran without warnings or errors:
avg.forb.fit<-sem(avg.forb.model,data=forb)

Code with group() that ran with error:
avg.forb.fit<-sem(avg.forb.model,group="site",data=forb)

messages.subject: Re: Configural model for longitudinal model with dichotomous data
messages.subject_clean: Configural model for longitudinal model with dichotomous data
messages.body_plain:
I agree with Felix that you should read Wu & Estabrook and follow their advice.  Millsap & Tein were not exploring the issue fully.  The goal of that dissertation project was merely to identify the model in ONE such a way (not all possible ways) that no latent means or variances needed to be constrained to equality across groups in the configural model.  But that is not remotely necessary as a criterion, as long as you are aware of what identification constraints should be released because they are not necessary once certain equality constraints are imposed.

Analogously, it is not necessary to use a marker variable with multivariate normal indicators.  You can fix the factor variances to 1 in the configural model for identification, as long as you remember to free all but one factor variance once you equate loadings.  The situation is simply more complicated with categorical indicators because the location/scale not only of latent common factors but also of latent item responses needs to be identified with constraints.  Millsap & Tein tried to simplify the issue by specifying a configural that required researchers to do nothing except add equality constraints to test invariance, but that simplification requires a complicated configural model that is statistically equivalent to the software defaults in Mplus and lavaan.  Wu & Estabrook (link below) explored the issue more completely, and in my opinion provide improved advice based on their more complete consideration of which measurement parameters can(not) be independently identified.  For example, Millsap & Tein simply ignored the issue of intercepts by assuming those were invariant.  But in Likert data (not binary, like yours) they can be separately identified from thresholds.  So it makes sense to test threshold equivalence before testing equivalence of loadings, intercepts, and residuals in the usual order we would follow with continuous data.  But with your binary data, testing equivalence of any type of measurement parameter requires assuming that the other three types are equivalent.

Anyway, the Millsap & Tein specification has trouble converging in R's optimizer that lavaan uses to estimate parameters, so if you can't get your model to run, that is another practical reason to consider using a different configural model that Millsap and Tein's.  But I do provide notes below to correct a few mistakes in your specification:

> fac2.1 =~ 1 * q1.1

I think lavaanify() strips all whitespace anyway, but for clarity of reading, I would not leave space between your modifier and the variable.

fac2.1 =~ 1*q1.1

> # latent common factor means
> fac2.1 ~ 0

To fix it to zero, this should be fac2.1 ~ 0*1

Think of "1" as the variable (actually the contant) on which fac2.1 is regressed, which provides estimation of the intercept (which is the grand mean when there are no other predictors).

> # thresholds, restrict threshold to be constant across time

Correct

> # residual covariances

Correct

> # residuals
> # fix for Time 1

Correct

> # force to be estimated for Times 2 & 3
> q1.2 ~~ NA * q1.2

Correct, BUT you need to fix the marker variable's variance to 1.
q1.2 ~~ 1*q1.2
q1.3 ~~ 1*q1.3

> # fix all intercepts to 0

Correct, but this will be automatically the case, so you don't need it in the syntax.  If you do, then just as for the latent means, you need to say what parameter is fixed to zero by putting 0 as a modifier to the ~1 parameter:

> q1.1 + q4.1 + q10.1 + q11.1 + q15.1 + q19.1 + q23.1 + q27.1 + q28.1 ~ 0*1
> q1.2 + q4.2 + q10.2 + q11.2 + q15.2 + q19.2 + q23.2 + q27.2 + q28.2 ~ 0*1
> q1.3 + q4.3 + q10.3 + q11.3 + q15.3 + q19.3 + q23.3 + q27.3 + q28.3 ~ 0*1

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Measurement invariance using a different number of Likert-type points
messages.subject_clean: Measurement invariance using a different number of Likert-type points
messages.body_plain:
> I would like to know if I'm able to test measurement invariance using three samples of the same instrument, one using 15 items with 1-5 answers, and the other two using 1-7 answers for the same 15 items. Thinking about the thresholds for categorical items MI I easily doubt about it, but nevertheless, someone can bring a different idea...

Well, if you treat the data as continuous (probably OK: http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf), then you just need to transform one set of anchors to correspond to the other anchor points.
To change a 1-7 scale to range from 1-5, multiple the 1-7 variable by 5/7
To change a 1-5 scale to range from 1-7, multiple the 1-5 variable by 7/5
If you want to treat them as categorical, then you have to consider which of the 4 of the 6 thresholds (in the 1-7 data) are supposed to be theoretically equal to the 4 thresholds in the 1-5 data.  Are only the anchor points defined (which I would argue puts the variables on a continuum, measured discretely) or is every ordinal category labeled?  If they are all labeled, then you can match category labels, and collapse the 7-point scale to 5 points by collapsing categories that only exist in the 7-point version.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: prediction for model without latent variables
messages.subject_clean: prediction for model without latent variables
messages.body_plain:
> my model doesn't use latent variables at all... when trying to predict with another dataset with lavPredict( ... type="yhat"/"ov", newdata=newdataset), I only get predictions for my indepentend variables and not for all, which I would need.

>
> (I don't fully get why this is the case, I guess it is due to some theory of computing predictions)

In lavaan, the predict() method is written for computing factor scores, not predicted values of observed variables.  This is because in covariance structure analysis, the "data" analyzed/explained/predicted is the covariance matrix and mean vector, not the N x P data table of cases by variables.  This is why the fitted() method returns the model-implied covariance matrix and mean vector in lavaan, whereas for the (g)lm function, it is redundant with the predict() method when no new data are passed for prediction.

What do you need the predicted values for?  If it is only a path analysis, then you can just fit a univariate multiple-regression model to each outcome with the (g)lm function, and pass your new data using the predict() methods for those objects.

Alternatively, Jarrett Byrnes wrote some code to provide predicted values of outcome variables from lavaan objects, which I hope to eventually incorporate into the semTools package (unless Yves plans to incorporate it into lavaan).  You can grab his code here and use it; hopefully it works.

https://github.com/jebyrnes/semTools/blob/master/semTools/R/fitted_lavaan.R

messages.body_plain:
> I am trying to set up a hierarchical SEM

What is that?  You syntax does not specify a higher-order common factor.

> a random effect.

If by hierarchical, you mean multilevel, then lavaan's limited multilevel capabilities cannot yet handle categorical data.

http://users.ugent.be/~yrosseel/lavaan/zurich2017/MULTILEVEL/lavaan_multilevel_zurich2017.pdf

> I think my current issue comes down to needing to use categorical variables that can't be ordered

You mean they are nominal variables?  If they are binary, you can consider them as ordinal because the distinction between an ordered vs. unordered pair of categories is only theoretical, but statistically equivalent (that is why we can use dummy codes as predictors in regression models, because a 1-unit "increase" merely means changing from one category to another).  lavaan does not support multicategory nominal outcomes.  If they are predictors, you need to make your own dummy codes to represent them.

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

messages.subject: Re: correlation between slopes, Latent growth modeling
messages.subject_clean: correlation between slopes, Latent growth modeling
messages.body_plain:
> Q1) I interpreted my PI's question to be asking about the correlation between slopes of PH and TNF. Does that make sense?

Sounds reasonable, that's how I would interpret it, too.

> Q2) Is multivariate latent growth curve modeling the most appropriate analytic strategy? I know there are other methods (repeated measure anova, panel models, etc.) to do longitudinal data, but do they answer if the longitudinal change in one variable is associated with the longitudinal change in the other?

Since you have nonlinear change of PH in one group, I think it is more complicated.  In the case of linear change, a single slope describes the change, so you can look at a single correlation between the latent slopes of PH and TNF.  But to model nonlinear change in the other group, it sounds like your expectations would be better suited to using latent difference scores, which are equivalent to having a latent "slope" at each time after baseline that merely represents change from baseline (you could also specify it to be change from the previous time, which is the usual application of latent difference scores).  Here is a good book:

http://www.longitudinalsem.com/

Anyway, in that case, you can't boil the "relationship" between the 2 change process down to a single correlation.  The change (linear slope?) in TNF will have a correlation between each latent-change factor used to represent nonlinear change in PH.  I suppose you could report each one, but talk to your PI about it.

> Q3) have I done the model specification properly?

You have 2 groups, so you need to specify both fixed values, even if it is the same fixed value:

i.PH =~ c(1, 1)*sq_phT1 + c(1, 1)*sq_phT2 + ...

And make sure to free parameters using NA, to make sure they are estimated, for example:

i.PH ~ c(NA, NA)*1

> #regressions
> s.PH ~ s.TNF
> i.PH ~ i.TNF
> '

Why as regressions?  You said you wanted the correlation, so just specify them as covariances (~~)

> the problem is that when i run it i get a warning. I believe because in the HC group the variance of the slope of PH is estimated as negative,

Correct

> Q4) have I done something wrong?

You have very small samples, so there is a lot of sampling variability in these estimates.  As you can see, the 95% CI includes positive values, so this negative-variance estimate is consistent with sampling error.

http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0049124112442138

> Variances:
>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|) ci.lower ci.upper   Std.lv  Std.all

>    .s.PH             -0.015    0.098   -0.156    0.876   -0.208    0.177      NaN      NaN

messages.body_plain:
> I have 17 sites that have multiple observations at each (less than 6 observations though)

Yikes!

> I did not have this error before including the group() command in the code. Any thoughts for why this might be?

Small Ns.  Possible, one of your variables is a constant within one of these groups.  Have you checked whether all of your variables vary within group?  (obviously, Level-2 variables would not vary within any Level-2 units, making them constants with 0 variance, hence the error)

aggregate(cbind(myFirstVariable, mySecondVariable, ...) ~ myGroupingVariable, data = forb, sd)

> Or any suggestions for how to control for repeated measurements at a site?

You haven't much information about your model, but you seem to want to estimate a growth model, so you have T repeated occasions nested within approximately 6*17 cases nested within 17 sites?  Have you considered estimating the growth curve as s 3-level model using lme() or lmer()?  An N = T*6*17 would not be so bad of a Level-1 sample size, although the higher-level Ns would still be small enough to be wary of the variance-component estimates.

messages.subject: Re: group equality constraint
messages.subject_clean: group equality constraint
messages.body_plain:
> According to package manual:
> group.equal
>
> A vector of character strings. Only used in a multiple group analysis. Can be one or more of the following:"loadings", "intercepts", "means", "regressions", "residuals" or "covariances", specifying the pattern of equality constraints across multiple groups.

Make sure you consult the latest version: http://lavaan.ugent.be/development.html

The options are:
"loadings", "intercepts", "means", "thresholds", "regressions", "residuals", "residual.covariances", "lv.variances" or "lv.covariances"

Note that these labels are meant to apply to common-factor (CFA) models, as shortcuts for testing measurement invariance.  They can be applied to path analyses and other types of SEM as well, but the labels correspond to parameter as they are interpreted in CFA.

> 1. loadings can be interpreted as the beta coefficients of a regression equation i.e. the lambda matrix

Correct, the lambdas, in LISREL notation, not the betas

> 2. intercepts can be interpreted as the alpha coefficient of a regression equation

of observed variables, yes (the tau vector in LISREL, or nu in Mplus and lavaan).  In CFA, observed variables are (only) endogenous indicators, but this refers to intercepts of observed variables in any type of model.

> 5. residuals: does this refer to the off diagonal of the theta θ (error) matrix or it refers to both the diagonals and the off diagonal elements of the theta θ (error) matrix?

Only the diagonal elements of theta.  "residual.covariances" refers (only) to off-diagonal elements of theta (regardless of the type of model; i.e., it does not constrain residual (co)variances of latent variables in structural regression models, for example).  Constraining latent (co)variances is similarly accomplished using "lv.variances" or "lv.covariances".

> 4. regressions: I have no idea what this means can anyone provide a suggestion regarding this?

Regressions among latent variables (the Beta matrix in LISREL)

> 3. means: does this refer to the mu matrix? however what is the difference between this and the intercepts situation profited that an intercept can be interpreted as the mean of one variable when the other variable is 0

This always refers to intercepts of latent variables (the alpha vector in LISREL notation).  In CFA, latent variables are exogenous, so their intercepts are means.  But in any type of SEM, this will constrain the latent intercepts.  Means (mu) are not model parameters, so they cannot be constrained without some clever syntax reproducing the model-implied means as user-defined parameters, then constraining those.

Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Confirmatory Factor Analysis with non-normal data and categorial items - Which estimator?
messages.subject_clean: Confirmatory Factor Analysis with non-normal data and categorial items - Which estimator?
messages.body_plain:
> Likert-scale from 0 to 10)

With so many ordered categories, this is approximately continuous:

> As I have a non-normal data, I cannot use ML as estimator

Yes you can, just use a robust correction.

> However, I cannot decide which estimator I should use instead. I have read about Unweighted Least Squares, Weighted Least Squares (or Asymptotic Distribution Free), Robust Weighted Least Squares (WLSMV) and MLM (Satorra-Bentler).
>
> First of all, I would really like to know which one is better and why.

You can't trust the SEs and test statistics from ULS, and you can only trust the ones from ADF if the sample size is in the thousands (you only have N=276), so avoid both of those.  WLSMV and MLM/MLR return similar results with so many ordered categories:

http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf

MLR has the advantage over MLM of being available even with missing data and you want to use FIML.  With complete data, MLM and MLR are asymptotically equivalent.

> And second, I would like to know what should I report for MLM and WLSMV as I have 2 columns in the summary (example here below for the MLM).

Use the robust column, which provides the robust-corrections to the naïve statistics in the left column.

> There's also a robust CFI and a robust TLI (the ones above, in the column robust were not the robust ones?!).

Those are only available with robust ML, but yes, refer to those instead of the "scaled" versions in the "Robust" column.  It is a little less confusing in the fitMeasures() output, which labels them as scaled vs. robust.  These articles explain why the Robust CFI, TLI, and RMSEA are better than simply calculating them using the scaled chi-squared value.

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2014.933697

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2012.715252

Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Thanks, will take a look at Wu & Estabrook (2016).

On Fri, May 4, 2018 at 4:58 AM, Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I agree with Felix that you should read Wu & Estabrook and follow their advice.  Millsap & Tein were not exploring the issue fully.  The goal of that dissertation project was merely to identify the model in ONE such a way (not all possible ways) that no latent means or variances needed to be constrained to equality across groups in the configural model.  But that is not remotely necessary as a criterion, as long as you are aware of what identification constraints should be released because they are not necessary once certain equality constraints are imposed.
>
> Analogously, it is not necessary to use a marker variable with multivariate normal indicators.  You can fix the factor variances to 1 in the configural model for identification, as long as you remember to free all but one factor variance once you equate loadings.  The situation is simply more complicated with categorical indicators because the location/scale not only of latent common factors but also of latent item responses needs to be identified with constraints.  Millsap & Tein tried to simplify the issue by specifying a configural that required researchers to do nothing except add equality constraints to test invariance, but that simplification requires a complicated configural model that is statistically equivalent to the software defaults in Mplus and lavaan.  Wu & Estabrook (link below) explored the issue more completely, and in my opinion provide improved advice based on their more complete consideration of which measurement parameters can(not) be independently identified.  For example, Millsap & Tein simply ignored the issue of intercepts by assuming those were invariant.  But in Likert data (not binary, like yours) they can be separately identified from thresholds.  So it makes sense to test threshold equivalence before testing equivalence of loadings, intercepts, and residuals in the usual order we would follow with continuous data.  But with your binary data, testing equivalence of any type of measurement parameter requires assuming that the other three types are equivalent.
>
> Anyway, the Millsap & Tein specification has trouble converging in R's optimizer that lavaan uses to estimate parameters, so if you can't get your model to run, that is another practical reason to consider using a different configural model that Millsap and Tein's.  But I do provide notes below to correct a few mistakes in your specification:
>
> > fac2.1 =~ 1 * q1.1
>
> I think lavaanify() strips all whitespace anyway, but for clarity of reading, I would not leave space between your modifier and the variable.
>
> fac2.1 =~ 1*q1.1
>
> > # latent common factor means
> > fac2.1 ~ 0
>
> To fix it to zero, this should be fac2.1 ~ 0*1
>
> Think of "1" as the variable (actually the contant) on which fac2.1 is regressed, which provides estimation of the intercept (which is the grand mean when there are no other predictors).
>
> > # thresholds, restrict threshold to be constant across time
>
> Correct
>
> > # residual covariances
>
> Correct
>
> > # residuals
> > # fix for Time 1
>
> Correct
>
> > # force to be estimated for Times 2 & 3
> > q1.2 ~~ NA * q1.2
>
> Correct, BUT you need to fix the marker variable's variance to 1.
> q1.2 ~~ 1*q1.2
> q1.3 ~~ 1*q1.3
>
> > # fix all intercepts to 0
>
> Correct, but this will be automatically the case, so you don't need it in the syntax.  If you do, then just as for the latent means, you need to say what parameter is fixed to zero by putting 0 as a modifier to the ~1 parameter:
>
> > q1.1 + q4.1 + q10.1 + q11.1 + q15.1 + q19.1 + q23.1 + q27.1 + q28.1 ~ 0*1
> > q1.2 + q4.2 + q10.2 + q11.2 + q15.2 + q19.2 + q23.2 + q27.2 + q28.2 ~ 0*1
> > q1.3 + q4.3 + q10.3 + q11.3 + q15.3 + q19.3 + q23.3 + q27.3 + q28.3 ~ 0*1

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to know if I am correctly specifying my models in the measurement invariance (MI) analysis.
If this is correct, then my MI analysis using the standardized factor/LV method is probably wrong. Because when I proceed to the weak invariant model and compare the configural to the weak model, then the degrees of freedom (df) differ for the two methods (i.e. effects coding vs standardization method).

### Configural model

Model1 <- '
# latent variables
Motivation0 =~ A1*V_0_1 + B1*V_0_3 + C1*V_0_4 + D1*V_0_5 + E1*V_0_6
Motivation1 =~ A2*V_1_1 + B2*V_1_3 + C2*V_1_4 + D2*V_1_5 + E2*V_1_6
Motivation3 =~ A3*V_3_1 + B3*V_3_3 + C3*V_3_4 + D3*V_3_5 + E3*V_3_6
Motivation4 =~ A4*V_4_1 + B4*V_4_3 + C4*V_4_4 + D4*V_4_5 + E4*V_4_6

# Item covariances

V_0_1 ~~ V_1_1 + V_3_1 + V_4_1
V_1_1 ~~ V_3_1 + V_4_1
V_3_1 ~~ V_4_1

V_0_3 ~~ V_1_3 + V_3_3 +  V_4_3
V_1_3 ~~ V_3_3 + V_4_3
V_3_3 ~~ V_4_3

V_0_4 ~~ V_1_4 + V_3_4 + V_4_4
V_1_4 ~~ V_3_4 + V_4_4
V_3_4 ~~ V_4_4

V_0_5 ~~ V_1_5 + V_3_5 + V_4_5
V_1_5 ~~ V_3_5 + V_4_5
V_3_5 ~~ V_4_5

V_0_6 ~~ V_1_6 + V_3_6 + V_4_6
V_1_6 ~~ V_3_6 + V_4_6
V_3_6 ~~ V_4_6

# Factor covariances

Motivation0 ~~ Motivation1 + Motivation3 + Motivation4
Motivation1 ~~ Motivation3 + Motivation4
Motivation3 ~~ Motivation4

# Constraint for effects coding (factor loadings)

A1 + B1 + C1 + D1 + E1 == 5
A2 + B2 + C2 + D2 + E2 == 5
A3 + B3 + C3 + D3 + E3 == 5
A4 + B4 + C4 + D4 + E4 == 5

# Intercepts items

V_0_1 ~ a1*1
V_1_1 ~ a2*1
V_3_1 ~ a3*1
V_4_1 ~ a4*1

V_0_3 ~ b1*1
V_1_3 ~ b2*1
V_3_3 ~ b3*1
V_4_3 ~ b4*1

V_0_4 ~ c1*1
V_1_4 ~ c2*1
V_3_4 ~ c3*1
V_4_4 ~ c4*1

V_0_5 ~ d1*1
V_1_5 ~ d2*1
V_3_5 ~ d3*1
V_4_5 ~ d4*1

V_0_6 ~ e1*1
V_1_6 ~ e2*1
V_3_6 ~ e3*1
V_4_6 ~ e4*1

# Constraint for effects coding (intercepts)

a1 + b1 + c1 + d1 + e1 == 0
a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 + e2 == 0
a3 + b3 + c3 + d3 + e3 == 0
a4 + b4 + c4 + d4 + e4 == 0

# Intercepts factors

Motivation0 ~ 1
Motivation1 ~ 1
Motivation3 ~ 1
Motivation4 ~ 1

'

fit1a <- lavaan(model = Model1, data = data, auto.var = TRUE)
summary(fit1a, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

#############
## WEAK INVARIANCE (fixed factor loadings over time)
#############

Model2 <- '
# latent variables
Motivation0 =~ A1*V_0_1 + B1*V_0_3 + C1*V_0_4 + D1*V_0_5 + E1*V_0_6
Motivation1 =~ A1*V_1_1 + B1*V_1_3 + C1*V_1_4 + D1*V_1_5 + E1*V_1_6

# Item covariances

V_0_1 ~~ V_1_1 + V_3_1 + V_4_1
V_1_1 ~~ V_3_1 + V_4_1
V_3_1 ~~ V_4_1

V_0_3 ~~ V_1_3 + V_3_3 +  V_4_3

V_3_4 ~~ V_4_4

V_0_5 ~~ V_1_5 + V_3_5 + V_4_5
V_1_5 ~~ V_3_5 + V_4_5

V_0_6 ~~ V_1_6 + V_3_6 + V_4_6
V_1_6 ~~ V_3_6 + V_4_6
V_3_6 ~~ V_4_6

# Factor covariances

Motivation0 ~~ Motivation1 + Motivation3 + Motivation4
Motivation1 ~~ Motivation3 + Motivation4
Motivation3 ~~ Motivation4

# Constraint for effects coding (factor loadings)
A1 + B1 + C1 + D1 + E1 == 5

# Intercepts observed variables
V_0_1 ~ a1*1
V_1_1 ~ a2*1
V_3_1 ~ a3*1
V_4_1 ~ a4*1

V_0_3 ~ b1*1
V_1_3 ~ b2*1
V_3_3 ~ b3*1
V_4_3 ~ b4*1

V_0_4 ~ c1*1
V_1_4 ~ c2*1
V_3_4 ~ c3*1
V_4_4 ~ c4*1

V_0_5 ~ d1*1
V_1_5 ~ d2*1
V_3_5 ~ d3*1
V_4_5 ~ d4*1

V_0_6 ~ e1*1
V_1_6 ~ e2*1
V_3_6 ~ e3*1
V_4_6 ~ e4*1

# constraint for effects coding (intercepts)
a1 + b1 + c1 + d1 + e1 == 0
a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 + e2 == 0
a3 + b3 + c3 + d3 + e3 == 0
a4 + b4 + c4 + d4 + e4 == 0

# Intercepts factors
Motivation0 ~ 1
Motivation1 ~ 1
Motivation3 ~ 1
Motivation4 ~ 1

'

fit2a <- lavaan(model = Model2, data = data, auto.var = TRUE)

Note: for the strong invariant model I would make the intercepts equal, so I would only have left the following:
 a1 + b1 + c1 + d1 + e1 == 0

Amonet

> > Nicolas,
> > I am not sure that you question has a matter of fact answer because it is a matter of accepted practice which may vary by literature.  Here are some thoughts.
> >
> > One thing that you could do is to extract the sample means, implied means, and mean residuals.  Plotting the first two against time might make a convincing case, particularly combined with the fact that the linear model does not reach a valid solution.
> >
> > One thing that I notice is that your variable names begin with 'sqr'.  If that stands for square root (or square) you might consider analyzing the variables without the transformation to see if the non-linearity goes away.
> >
> > You are somewhat limited by having only four time points.  In future studies, if you can collect more time points, you might consider adding a second slope that has fixed zero loadings up until the time point represented by your 3rd time point and then has a linear slope (piecewise growth) or adding a second slope affecting all time points with loadings equal to the square of the linear loadings (quadratic polynomial growth).  Free loadings are not really testing a specific nonlinear hypothesis but just an unspecific alternative hypothesis to the linear null.
> >
> > You could try constraining the variances to be non-negative and refitting the linear growth model.  I think that it is fair to say that majority opinion has come down on the side that this is not good general practice because it tends to hide problems with the model.  However, in your situation, it may be a useful follow-up to fitting the model without the non-negativitiy constraints.  It might not converge at all but it if does it may give you a poorly fitting solution that passes basic admissibility tests.
> >
> > I am not a statistician but it seems to me that the following logic holds.  The inadmissible solution represents the best obtainable fit (assuming you get a consistent solution) for the unconstrained linear growth model.  As such, any admissible solution would have to fit worse.  So, if the nonlinear growth model fits better at a statistically significant level, then it must also fit better than any admissible solution for the linear growth model.  However, it may be helpful to compare the inadmissible solution to an admissible solution with constraints, because you would not accept the inadmissible solution even if it fit well, or within sampling error of the non-linear growth model.  Perhaps others can comment on the behavior of chi-square for inadmissible solutions and the validity of such chi-square difference tests.

messages.body_plain:
Amonet,
  Yes, these are the residuals for the sample moments, not individual values of variables.  This is why I like to put the non-redundant off-diagonal values in a stem-and-leaf plot.  If you have a small model with few observed variables, there is less to go on.  With larger models, you have more residuals to work with.

  When Todd cautions about heavy tails, he is referring to a pattern of residuals that are larger than would be expected by random normal deviations.  Skewness also suggests a pattern of larger-than-expected residuals in the tail.  Likewise an outlier is a larger-than-expected residual that appears outside the distribution.  The describe() function in the psych package offers a convenient way to obtain numeric summary statistics for univariate distributions.

Keith

Oh the basic solution was that the model was mis-specified.

Originally, i forced the slope into a linear trend (i.e. s.PH =~ 0*sqrev_phT1 + 1*sqrev_phT2 + 3*sqrev_phT3 + 4*sqrev_phT4).

I then tried to let it freely estimate (i.e. s.PH =~ 0*sqrev_phT1 + 1*sqrev_phT2 + ?*sqrev_phT3 + ?*sqrev_phT4) which suggested a non-linear trend (specifically --  s.PH =~ 0*sqrev_phT1 + 1*sqrev_phT2 + .5*sqrev_phT3 + .5*sqrev_phT4). Once i used either the free estimation or the non-linear trend it solved the issue.

I believe (and someone please correct me if i am wrong), that between the small sample size I have to work with, and the misspecification, it caused the estimated negative lv variance

> > > Nicolas,
> > > I am not sure that you question has a matter of fact answer because it is a matter of accepted practice which may vary by literature.  Here are some thoughts.
> > >
> > > One thing that you could do is to extract the sample means, implied means, and mean residuals.  Plotting the first two against time might make a convincing case, particularly combined with the fact that the linear model does not reach a valid solution.
> > >
> > > One thing that I notice is that your variable names begin with 'sqr'.  If that stands for square root (or square) you might consider analyzing the variables without the transformation to see if the non-linearity goes away.
> > >
> > > You are somewhat limited by having only four time points.  In future studies, if you can collect more time points, you might consider adding a second slope that has fixed zero loadings up until the time point represented by your 3rd time point and then has a linear slope (piecewise growth) or adding a second slope affecting all time points with loadings equal to the square of the linear loadings (quadratic polynomial growth).  Free loadings are not really testing a specific nonlinear hypothesis but just an unspecific alternative hypothesis to the linear null.
> > >
> > > You could try constraining the variances to be non-negative and refitting the linear growth model.  I think that it is fair to say that majority opinion has come down on the side that this is not good general practice because it tends to hide problems with the model.  However, in your situation, it may be a useful follow-up to fitting the model without the non-negativitiy constraints.  It might not converge at all but it if does it may give you a poorly fitting solution that passes basic admissibility tests.
> > >
> > > I am not a statistician but it seems to me that the following logic holds.  The inadmissible solution represents the best obtainable fit (assuming you get a consistent solution) for the unconstrained linear growth model.  As such, any admissible solution would have to fit worse.  So, if the nonlinear growth model fits better at a statistically significant level, then it must also fit better than any admissible solution for the linear growth model.  However, it may be helpful to compare the inadmissible solution to an admissible solution with constraints, because you would not accept the inadmissible solution even if it fit well, or within sampling error of the non-linear growth model.  Perhaps others can comment on the behavior of chi-square for inadmissible solutions and the validity of such chi-square difference tests.

Joshin,
  Notice the near zero R-square values for reli1 to reli4.  That suggests that these variables have nothing in common and do not serve as indicators of the same latent variable.  To test this out, look at the correlation matrix for your data.  Then use the itemanal() function in the rela package to obtain rest-score correlations and R-squares.  (Note that itemanal() has a quirk that it requires a matrix with names.  Converting a data frame to a matrix will satisfy this requirement.)

require(rela)
round(cor(wddata),3)
itemanal(as.matrix(wddata[c('reli1', 'reli2', 'reli3', 'reli4')]))

If these results confirm the idea that the four variables are not related to one another, then consider dropping the RelAf latent variable and allowing them to have direct effects on wlb.

messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody,

I am using lavaan to analyze the results of an experiment which included 2 binary categorical predictors ('strategies' and 'evidence'), 3 endogenous dependent variables (benevolence, integrity and credibility) and two exogenous control variables (distrust and orientation), one of which, i.e. orientation, was measured using a single-item scale.

This is how I've defined my model in lavaan.

full_SEM <- '

# latent variable definitions

  benevolence =~ Q2_1 + Q2_2 + Q2_3

  integrity =~ Q3_1 + Q3_2 + Q3_4

  credibility =~ Q4_1 + Q4_2 + Q4_3

  distrust =~ Q5_1 + Q5_2 + Q5_3 + Q5_4

# regressions

  benevolence ~ strategies + evidence + distrust + orientation

  integrity ~ strategies + evidence + distrust + orientation

  credibility ~ benevolence + integrity + evidence + distrust + orientation

# variable correlations

  benevolence ~~ integrity

  distrust ~~ orientation

'

This is the function I used to fit the model.

SEM_model_fit <- sem(full_SEM, data = SEM_data, fixed.x = T)

I have two issues:

1. I used the argument 'fixed.x = T' because the model includes two experimental variables which should not be correlated with each other, given that they were randomly distributed among the participants. However, when I run the fitting command above, I get this error message:

Warning message:

In lavaan::lavaan(model = full_SEM, data = SEM_data, fixed.x = T,  :

  lavaan WARNING: syntax contains parameters involving exogenous covariates; switching to fixed.x = FALSE

It looks like the parameter 'fixed.x = T' is overridden. Does anybody know why this may be the case? Could this be caused by the single-item scale?

2. The results of the analysis include the estimates for the intercorrelations between the experimental variables, which should not actually be considered.

Covariances:

                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all

.benevolence ~~

   .integrity         0.820    0.099    8.268    0.000    0.696    0.696

  distrust ~~

    orientation      -0.271    0.080   -3.391    0.001   -0.311   -0.224

  strategies ~~

    evidence         -0.009    0.015   -0.637    0.524   -0.009   -0.037

How can I therefore exclude intercorrelation between experimental variables in lavaan?

Thanks so much in advance for your generous help!

Matteo Fuoli

(University of Birmningham)

messages.body_plain:
Matteo,
  I think that I see the logic in what you did.  Removing a parameter from the model means different things in different contexts.  It can mean fixing the parameter to zero, which is what you wanted.  However, in the context of fixed.x, it means not attempting to model a portion of the data.  That is not what you were trying to do although it might still make sense for you.

  To fix a covariance to zero, use something like this in your model specification:

strategies ~~ 0*evidence

  Notice that the covariance estimated in your model is near zero and not statistically significantly different from zero.  Estimating a zero parameter will not introduce bias.  It just eats a degree of freedom.

  As an alternative, you could follow the fixed.x strategy.  This will not fix the values inside the model.  Instead, it removes the variances and inter-covariances between exogenous variables from the moments to which the model is fit.  The values are simply read off the data.  So, they cannot be fixed to zero.  However they do not count for or against the degrees of freedom.

  The problem with your attempt appears to the the covariance between distrust and orientation.  Both of these are exogenous variables.  So, if you want to used fixed.x, you should omit this line from your model specification.  When lavaan finds a parameter that is not part of the fixed.x model, it switches back to the full model to accommodate that parameter.

Keith

------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

Amonet,
  Off the top of my head, I do not see a reason that the df should differ between parameterizations.  In the configural model, each fixed unit loading in the first parameterization corresponds to an effects coding constraint in the second parameterization.  When you impose equality constraints across times, all but one of the fixed unit loadings becomes redundant.  Likewise, all but one of the effects coding constraints becomes redundant.  Everything else should stay the same, unless I am missing something.

  Perhaps it would be best to work with a minimal example, perhaps 2 times and 4 indicators, to work out the conceptual issues.  Then ramp up to the full model once you solve the problem.  It is hard to guess why you are obtaining different df without seeing both parameterizations.  If the reason for the difference does not jump out at you working with smaller models, perhaps you could post just the models that differ in df (presumably either the configural or the weak invariance models) and the df count for each.  That would give us something more concrete with which to work.

Keith

> > > > Nicolas,
> > > > I am not sure that you question has a matter of fact answer because it is a matter of accepted practice which may vary by literature.  Here are some thoughts.
> > > >
> > > > One thing that you could do is to extract the sample means, implied means, and mean residuals.  Plotting the first two against time might make a convincing case, particularly combined with the fact that the linear model does not reach a valid solution.
> > > >
> > > > One thing that I notice is that your variable names begin with 'sqr'.  If that stands for square root (or square) you might consider analyzing the variables without the transformation to see if the non-linearity goes away.
> > > >
> > > > You are somewhat limited by having only four time points.  In future studies, if you can collect more time points, you might consider adding a second slope that has fixed zero loadings up until the time point represented by your 3rd time point and then has a linear slope (piecewise growth) or adding a second slope affecting all time points with loadings equal to the square of the linear loadings (quadratic polynomial growth).  Free loadings are not really testing a specific nonlinear hypothesis but just an unspecific alternative hypothesis to the linear null.
> > > >
> > > > You could try constraining the variances to be non-negative and refitting the linear growth model.  I think that it is fair to say that majority opinion has come down on the side that this is not good general practice because it tends to hide problems with the model.  However, in your situation, it may be a useful follow-up to fitting the model without the non-negativitiy constraints.  It might not converge at all but it if does it may give you a poorly fitting solution that passes basic admissibility tests.
> > > >
> > > > I am not a statistician but it seems to me that the following logic holds.  The inadmissible solution represents the best obtainable fit (assuming you get a consistent solution) for the unconstrained linear growth model.  As such, any admissible solution would have to fit worse.  So, if the nonlinear growth model fits better at a statistically significant level, then it must also fit better than any admissible solution for the linear growth model.  However, it may be helpful to compare the inadmissible solution to an admissible solution with constraints, because you would not accept the inadmissible solution even if it fit well, or within sampling error of the non-linear growth model.  Perhaps others can comment on the behavior of chi-square for inadmissible solutions and the validity of such chi-square difference tests.

A correlation is a standardized covariance.  You standardize the covariance between X and Y by dividing it by the SD of X and the SD of Y. messages.body_plain:
> I got covariance estimates for ALL the exogenous variables in the model ! (even if I only asked for cov(Esteem10, ParInt10))...

sem() will do that by default, because it is a reasonable assumption that exogenous variables (i.e., variables explained outside your model) almost certainly have nonzero correlations, unless they were made to be orthogonal by design (e.g., randomly assigned treatment conditions with equal sample sizes).

> Is this normal/what people should usually do? what this mean substantially?

Yes

> and ..can I leave the analysis like that and interpreting the coefficients I'm interested in (in the regression table) without this interfering with them?

Yes, if you force them to be zero when their observed correlations are not zero, that will make you model fit worse.  By default, you don't even need to estimate exogenous (co)variances.  The argument fixed.x=TRUE (described on the ?lavOptions help page) means you just use the observed sample statistics in place of ML estimates of exogenous (co)variances, so it won't affect your model's df or fit.

> is there a specific method for doing this?

Your first specification is called a bifactor model, and would require constraining Text to be uncorrelated with Textmat and Textsoc.  The second specification is called a hierarchical, or second-order, factor model, and it would require fixing both Textmat and Textsoc loadings on Text to 1 to freely estimate the variance of Text (which is statistically equivalent to the covariance between Textmat and Textsoc if you left Text out of the model). messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Some context: I am doing a measurement invariance analysis and noticed that the strong invariant model is not fully supported by the chi-square difference test (p =.025), relative to the weak invariant model. Note that my sample size is quite small (roughly 120 individuals measured at 4 time points), so the test might lack power and thus even be on the large side here. Although the difference in CFI is <.01 (i.e. 0.0072), and the AIC actually improves (i.e. a decrease of 0.72 in the more restricted (strong) model), I thought it would be good to be on the safe side and release some of the imposed constraints of the strong invariant model. To this end I am using the lavTestscore() function and what I understand from here <https://rstudio-pubs-static.s3.amazonaws.com/194879_192b64ad567743d392b559d650b95a3b.html>, is that the lavTestscore applies a multivariate score test (or Lagrange multiplier test) and that if this turns out non-significant, none of the constraints should be released. This is sort of 'problematic' for me, as the objective is to study the latent means over time.

In my analysis this is the case: the multivariate score test is non-significant (p = .42), while the strong model may not be preferred over the weak model (see above).
However, there are some univariate score tests that are borderline significant (e.g., p =.048). Am I conducting a 'proper statistical analysis' if I would turn to these univariate tests, while the multivariate test indicates non-significance? In the end, here I might lack power also due to small sample size... this time "not in my favour".

With this, I have a question on how to interpret the output. Please see the picture of the output below (red marks indicate the 3 borderline significant tests):

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-D4ISpa8r38c/WvcjP3bGxMI/AAAAAAAAC7w/3j1Nn8-ldEQIXGTASwco-r_yafaBTgkuACLcBGAs/s1600/Knipsel.PNG>

Now, when I use partable() to find out with which constraints these 3 tests are associated with, I don't understand what they represent:

\

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-tBYuOrqqRW0/Wvcj3vYhB0I/AAAAAAAAC78/SQ0YUgT7Hg8kDttt_kfx8pHnSI4hs3dTACLcBGAs/s1600/Knipsel.PNG>

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-RqfIG0uVpfE/WvckIhVMLXI/AAAAAAAAC8E/kL3H8zY3FmshaU5z84ietnUQg_8-K8XTgCLcBGAs/s1600/Knipsel.PNG>

I didn't name anything .p##. myself, so I guess it's done internally.

Lastly, I had thought that if the test would fail, that at least some intercepts (that I imposed to be equal over time) would pop up in the univariate tests. After all, that's the only thing that was changed between the weak and strong model. Where could I go from here to potentially show partial strong invariance?

Any help will be appreciated.
Thank you,
Amonet

messages.body_plain:
> I understood why we should estimate the covariance of exogenous variables..but in my specific case is it not quite redundant?

Redundant with what?  Your syntax?  Yes, specifying that exogenous covariance in your model syntax would be redundant if you used the default fixed.x=TRUE because that information only needs to be taken as-is from the sample statistics.  An advantage of setting fixed.x=FALSE to estimate the exogenous parameters would be to use all available information (when using missing="fiml") if there are missing data even on the predictors.

> I've put almost all of the exogenous variables in both regression analyses, and as far as I know the main "job" of regression is accounting for the covariance between predictors ( and then see if what is left influence Y)..am I right?

I think the main job of regression is predicting an outcome, not explaining relationships among the predictors.  But the predictors are allowed to be correlated even in OLS regression -- those correlations just aren't estimated.  Path analysis is more complicated because you can have not only multiple (residually correlated) outcomes but also sequences of causal effects.  So you might be interested not only in predicting each outcome, but also seeing whether outcomes still have residual correlations after accounting for shared explanatory predictors (perhaps even seeing how much of the outcomes' covariance is explained).

But these are general questions that are not specific to lavaan.  You can find more feedback for questions like this on SEMNET:

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

messages.body_plain:
> In my analysis this is the case: the multivariate score test is non-significant (p = .42), while the strong model may not be preferred over the weak model (see above).

The multivariate score test is not comparing your weak and strong models.  It is testing all the constraints listed in the univariate tests output, which include both loadings and intercepts, so it is closer to comparing your configural and strong models.  But you already performed the omnibus test using a likelihood ratio test, so you don't need to pay attention to the multivariate score test (unless you have a hypothesis about freeing multiple particular constraints, in which case you should run lavTestScore() and specify only those constraints).  Just look at the univariate follow-up tests.

> However, there are some univariate score tests that are borderline significant (e.g., p =.048). Am I conducting a 'proper statistical analysis' if I would turn to these univariate tests, while the multivariate test indicates non-significance?

No, but you did not specify only the intercept constraints when you run lavTestScore().  To get the correct omnibus test, you can run (assuming the intercept constraints are in rows 18 through 32 of the univariate tests):

lavTestScore(fit, release = 18:32)

But again, you already tested the omnibus null hypothesis that all intercept-constraints hold in the population.  The score test is asymptotically equivalent to the LRT you already performed by comparing the weak and strong models.

https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.1982.10482817

Also, the "proper" type of analysis you are hoping to perform, if you use alpha = 5% for your omnibus test, then conduct several follow-up tests, you should adjust for the number of tests to control the familywise Type I error rate (e.g., a Bonferroni adjustment, dividing alpha by the number of intercept-contraints you test following your LRT).

> Now, when I use partable() to find out with which constraints these 3 tests are associated with, I don't understand what they represent: I didn't name anything .p##. myself, so I guess it's done internally.

Yes, those are the labels lavaan creates, using the parameter number in the "id" column.  .p1. == .p6. means those factor loadings are constrained to equality (evidenced by the .p1. label also appearing in the "label" column for each loading that is constrained to be equal to it).

So when you see the univariate score test labeled .p1. == .p6., that is a test of that particular constraint.

> Lastly, I had thought that if the test would fail, that at least some intercepts (that I imposed to be equal over time) would pop up in the univariate tests. After all, that's the only thing that was changed between the weak and strong model. Where could I go from here to potentially show partial strong invariance?

Well, the only 2 significant univariate tests are both associated with the intercept labeled .p57., although neither of them would be significant if you took steps to control your Type I error rate.  To perform fewer tests (and have more power), you could run only 1 post-hoc test of that item's intercepts:

lavTestScore(fit, release = 18:20)

If that particular 3-df post-hoc test is significant, release those constraints and compare the partial-strong model to the weak model using a LRT.

Also see my post on using EPCs and EPC-interest (e.g., how much do latent means differ if those 3 constraints are freed?) as an effect-size/impact criterion rather than statistical significance:  https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/fzIg5jrxIAI/xoq5l803AAAJ

Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

install.packages("lavaan", repos="http://www.da.ugent.be", type="source")
devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

> This is the configural model where I manually standardised the four latent variables (Motivation0, Motivation1, 3, 4). Is this normal or known to happen in Lavaan, or am I doing something wrong?

Nothing wrong.  Those are fixed parameters, so don't test them.  It is a numerical machine-precision issue that only happens when you constrain a label to a value (e.g., V==1) instead of fixing it to that value (e.g., Motivation ~~ 1*Motivation).  Sometimes the machine-precision error is large enough (e.g., only 1.000... out to the 15th decimal place instead of the 17th) that the optimizer might stop at a solution a little further away from the exact constraint, but not far enough to be of any practical significance.  That's why you get the same results as setting std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE.

Ilaria,

Yes, that's a lot. It sounds like you're doing a mediation model using lavaan to test whether a model with a direct path is better than a model without the direct path. Is this correct?

If so, you would have to report the following at a minimum:

1. Model fit statistics for both models
2. Chi-square difference test
3. All paths in your most significant model.
4. Estimated variance explained in your variables.
5. If using latent variables, a measurement model where you say whether you have good measurement or not.

In terms of best practices, what the other two posters have said to include should also be included as well.

Kline has a textbook that discusses reporting practices in SEM. Others have some as well online. Yes, it is a lot to report, but doing so gives the full picture. Alternatively, you can see recent published articles using the same technique that you are using and see what they report.

messages.subject: (first) release candidate lavaan 0.6-1
messages.subject_clean: (first) release candidate lavaan 0.6-1
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan users,

I have rolled up a 'release candidate' for lavaan 0.6-1. To install this version, type in R:

install.packages("lavaan", repos="http://www.da.ugent.be", type="source")

and it should be version 0.6-1.1239 (or higher). Please give it a try and reply to this thread to report any issues.

If you want to 'return' to the current CRAN version (0.5-23), you can just type

install.packages("lavaan")

again (and restart your R session), so it is perfectly safe to try out a dev version.

What is new?

- two-level SEM (continuous data, random intercepts only). Documentation
is on its way, but for now, see the following set of slides (eg slide 62
+ 63):

http://users.ugent.be/~yrosseel/lavaan/zurich2017/MULTILEVEL/lavaan_multilevel_zurich2017.pdf

- a complete rewrite of the code to compute (robust) standard errors and
(robust) test statistics; the code is now much more consistent, but this
may result in small changes in the values of some robust test statistics
as printed in the output of summary(); a meanstructure is no longer
added automatically

- conditional.x = FALSE works in the categorical case

- if fixed.x = TRUE, we compute the loglikelihood without the exogenous
covariates, and we do not allow for missing values in the exogenous
covariates when missing = "ml"

- estimator = "PML" now works for continuous-only data, or mixed
continuous/ordinal data

- many, many small changes under the hood.

If no major issues are found, we will upload lavaan 0.6-1 in a week or so.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
> Yes, my understanding is that 'std.all' is the standardized coefficient or the  semipartial correlation coefficient

Those 2 things are not generally the same, although in practice they are often very close.

> and it's square is the unique portion of variance explained by that variable.

That is the case for the semipartial correlation, but not the standardized slope.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: How to set up strict invariance for categorical variables
messages.body_plain:
> But, the parameters of residuals are still not constrained equally. Could you please let me know how to run  strict invariance ?

The default in lavaan is parameterization = "delta", which identifies latent item-responses by fixing the total variances to 1.  Upon constraining thresholds, that identification constraint can be released in all but one group/occasion, so other total variances can be estimated.  But the delta parameterization does not allow you to do anything about residual variances because those are fixed relative to whatever the total variance is.

https://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf

To instead fix the residual variances to 1 for identification in the configural model, use parameterization = "theta" (also described in the link above).  Then, when you constrain thresholds, the residual variances can be freely estimated in all but one group.  To test strict invariance, you cannot simply set estimates to be equal across groups because they are not estimated in the first group at all.  Because they are fixed to 1 in the first group for identification, you test strict invariance by fixing them to 1 in all groups.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

So, to be clear, if have A ~ B + C + D and I want the semipartial correlation^2 for B, I would need to run A~0*B+C+D? Wouldn't that remove the sum of explained variance unique to B + shared B-C + shared B-D components? So then, A~ B + 0*C + 0*D seems like it would deliver just the portion of explained variance unique to B?

On Thursday, May 17, 2018 at 12:50:17 PM UTC-5, TBP wrote:
> Thanks! You first answer reassures me that I am not completely clueless (just a somewhat), your second answer gives me the way forward!
>

> > > here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/lavaan/0ZUwUmXmIq0 you seem to suggest that the standardized coefficient, 'std.all', is the semipartial correlation coefficient
> >
> > That was a mistake, I have since learned :-)
> >
> > > So how do I get semipartial correlation coefficients that I can present as an r2?
> >
> > You could run a model with and without an effect, and compare their R-squared values.  The change in R-squared is the squared semipartial correlation of the effect you fixed to zero.
> >
> > Terrence D. Jorgensen
> > Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> > Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> > UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
> >

messages.body_plain:
Dear Lavaan users,
I'm getting trouble with the problem of ordered variables in SEM with Lavaan. I don't know whether it is a problem with the program or with my model. Let met describe my model.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-8sv9VtDGVTs/Wv9eXurp8OI/AAAAAAAABAE/5UkMA2h_FQkxTaqLdOJMoasqZrjaEpecQCLcBGAs/s1600/Untitled.jpg>

I attached the Lavaan.csv data file for this model with 200 samples. This is my code:

library(lavaan)
Table <- read.csv("Lavaan.csv",header = TRUE,sep = ",",dec = ".")
M<-as.matrix(Table)

#Run model with continuous variables
model <- '
y1 =~ x1
y2 =~ x2
y3 =~ x3 + x4 + x5
y4 =~ x6 + x7 + x8
y5 =~ x9
y6 =~ x10 + x11
# regressions
y1 ~ y3 + y5
y3 ~ y2 + y4 + y5 + y6
y2 ~ y6
y4 ~ y6
#Correlation
y2 ~~ y4
y2 ~~ y5
y4 ~~ y5
'
fit <- sem(model,sample.nobs = 200,estimator = "DWLS",data=M,std.lv=TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit,c("CFI","TLI","RMSEA","GFI","NFI","SRMR"))

All of my observed variables (indicators) are from a 5-points Likert scale. In the first attempt, I treated all of them as continous variables, then I run the model with DWLS estimator and the model is identified with very good fit.

> fit <- sem(model,sample.nobs = 200,estimator = "DWLS",data=M,std.lv=TRUE)
> fitMeasures(fit,c("CFI","TLI","RMSEA","GFI","NFI","SRMR"))
  cfi   tli rmsea   gfi   nfi  srmr
1.000 1.011 0.000 0.990 0.978 0.056

However, when I consider these variables as categorical variables by defining them as "ordered", the model was not identified:

#Run model with categorical variables

#Define ordered variables
M<- data.frame(M)
M$x1 <- ordered(M$x1,levels = c("1","2","3","4","5"))
M$x2 <- ordered(M$x2,levels = c("1","2","3","4","5"))
M$x3 <- ordered(M$x3,levels = c("1","2","3","4","5"))
M$x4 <- ordered(M$x4,levels = c("1","2","3","4","5"))
M$x5 <- ordered(M$x5,levels = c("1","2","3","4","5"))
M$x6 <- ordered(M$x6,levels = c("1","2","3","4","5"))
M$x7 <- ordered(M$x7,levels = c("1","2","3","4","5"))
M$x8 <- ordered(M$x8,levels = c("1","2","3","4","5"))
M$x9 <- ordered(M$x9,levels = c("1","2","3","4","5"))
M$x10 <- ordered(M$x10,levels = c("1","2","3","4","5"))
M$x11 <- ordered(M$x11,levels = c("1","2","3","4","5"))

fit <- sem(model,sample.nobs = 200,estimator = "DWLS",data=M,std.lv=TRUE)

Here is the result of the model with categorical variables:

> fit <- sem(model,sample.nobs = 200,estimator = "DWLS",data=M,std.lv=TRUE)
Warning messages:
1: In lav_samplestats_from_data(lavdata = lavdata, missing = lavoptions$missing,  :
  lavaan WARNING: 54 bivariate tables have empty cells; to see them, use:
                  lavInspect(fit, "zero.cell.tables")
2: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING: could not compute standard errors!
  lavaan NOTE: this may be a symptom that the model is not identified.

3: In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables
                is not positive definite;
                use inspect(fit,"cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") to investigate.

So this is what I cannot understand. Why with the same model, changing from continous variables to categorical variables cause the model from identified to unidentified? Is there any wrong in my syntax?

As I understand, the empty cell error in the bivariate table does not affect the identification.

Another question, if the variables are considered as continuous, is it possible to still use DWLS estimator instead of WLS estimator? My data is not multinormal so I cannot use ML estimator. When I switch to WLS, the model fit decrease significantly

> fit <- sem(model,sample.nobs = 200,estimator = "WLS",data=M,std.lv=TRUE)
> fitMeasures(fit,c("CFI","TLI","RMSEA","GFI","NFI","SRMR"))
  cfi   tli rmsea   gfi   nfi  srmr
0.670 0.481 0.107 0.904 0.613 0.215

Thank you very very much for taking time with my case. It was stressed with this problem. If variables cannot be considered as categorical, I have to use WLS estimator. However if I use WLS estimator, the model fit is very low (e.g. cfi at 0.67) and it suggests a bad model.

Best regads,

Tran Viet Yen.

> Hi,
>
> Some context: I am doing a measurement invariance analysis and noticed that the strong invariant model is not fully supported by the chi-square difference test (p =.025), relative to the weak invariant model. Note that my sample size is quite small (roughly 120 individuals measured at 4 time points), so the test might lack power and thus even be on the large side here. Although the difference in CFI is <.01 (i.e. 0.0072), and the AIC actually improves (i.e. a decrease of 0.72 in the more restricted (strong) model), I thought it would be good to be on the safe side and release some of the imposed constraints of the strong invariant model. To this end I am using the lavTestscore() function and what I understand from here <https://rstudio-pubs-static.s3.amazonaws.com/194879_192b64ad567743d392b559d650b95a3b.html>, is that the lavTestscore applies a multivariate score test (or Lagrange multiplier test) and that if this turns out non-significant, none of the constraints should be released. messages.subject_clean: Error While Modeling
messages.body_plain:
Generally, negative variances of observed variables (Heywood cases) are a sign that the model is wrongly specified.  The program says "I found a best solution, but that best solution cannot exist in the real world". Your model fit is also not great, which also suggests that the model could be better.

However, in your case the negative variances are not statistically significant. You might just ignore them, or you might constrain those variances to zero or a very small positive number - that should not hurt your model fit (much), but you should still convince yourself that the results are correct.

I'm surprised that AMOS gives a different result - are the other parameter estimates (and fit indices) the same?

messages.body_plain:
Joseph,
  The answer Jeremy gave is the consensus advice and the advice that I would have given had he not gotten there first.  However, in reading the thread, it occurs to me that assuming that a unique variance equals zero has a qualitative impact on a factor model.  It basically denies the central assumption that the factor is a latent variable.  So, while the consensus advice makes sense from the perspective of frequntist hypothesis testing, it might make sense from the perspective of theoretical inference to instead fix the negative unique variances to a small positive value.  This would allow you to test a model in which the unique variances are near zero but the factors are still latent variables.  A small positive value is quantitatively more different from your negative estimates than is zero, but it is theoretically less different from your initial hypothesis about how the items work.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

Hello,

First, thank you so much for the advice and direction Terrence, it was of great help. I got the Newsome book and the latent difference score models work great.

I do have some follow up questions though,

I still want to compare to groups, and I can write the code to run it, but I am curious how to apply some of the difference score analyses the book suggets. For example, setting the means of the latent change scores to be the same will allow the use of the chi-square test statistic to serve as something of a test for if the change is the same across between all time points (i.e. linear change). My question is how to apply this to multigroup analysis.

below is my code and output for an analysis.

I have set the means to be the same within each subgroup (a for group1 and b for group2), so that i can determine if there is an argument for assuming linearity or not. I can then run a dual latent difference score model with two variables that change over time, and correlate their difference scores at each time point to assess their relationship across time, within each group.

However, I am not sure now what/how i should be interpreting the chi-squares for the model information.

Q1) is the minimum test statistic being non-significant now suggest that the model fits better keeping the groups separated?
Q2) would i look at the individual group chi-square and as the measure of if there is a difference in the differences across time? i.e. for group1 chi-square =  5.061. if that is over the critical value (see Q3) it would be significant, which would suggest that the difference scores are not equivalent across time.
Q3) how do i go about determining the df for that chi-square? my guess is # difference scores - 1...but i am not sure

Any additional help would be wonderful. Thank you, and sorry again for the long post.

messages.subject_clean: Sum of semipartial r2 values greater than R2?
messages.body_plain:
> I want the semipartial correlation^2 for B, I would need to run A~0*B+C+D?

Yes, and compare that to the unrestricted model's R-squared.

> Wouldn't that remove the sum of explained variance unique to B + shared B-C + shared B-D components?

No, C and D are still predictors.  So whatever they have in common with B is still used to predict A.

> So then, A~ B + 0*C + 0*D seems like it would deliver just the portion of explained variance unique to B?

No, that would deliver the portion explainable by B without taking into account how much of that could also be explained by C and D.  So that R-squared would be the squared zero-order correlation between B and A.

messages.body_plain:
> Q1) is the minimum test statistic being non-significant now suggest that the model fits better keeping the groups separated?

The test statistic for a model is testing whether that model fits as well as a saturated model (i.e., freely estimating all possible means and (co)variances).  It is not comparing that model to any other restricted/hypothesized model.

> Q2) would i look at the individual group chi-square and as the measure of if there is a difference in the differences across time? i.e. for group1 chi-square =  5.061. if that is over the critical value (see Q3) it would be significant, which would suggest that the difference scores are not equivalent across time.

The group contributions to the chi-squared are not test statistics, so you cannot use them to test any hypothesis.

> Q3) how do i go about determining the df for that chi-square? my guess is # difference scores - 1...but i am not sure

The df for the test is listed with the test statistic. In order to test a particular hypothesis, you need to specify a model under which the null hypothesis is true (e.g., constrain differences to be equal, implying linearity) and a model under which the null is false (i.e., without the constraint), then compare those models using the anova() function, which returns a chi-squared difference test (along with its df).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Hi Terrence,
Thanks for helping me out.

> Also, the "proper" type of analysis you are hoping to perform, if you use alpha = 5% for your omnibus test, then conduct several follow-up tests, you should adjust for the number of tests to control the familywise Type I error rate (e.g., a Bonferroni adjustment, dividing alpha by the number of intercept-contraints you test following your LRT).

Thus, if I would test to release all intercepts constraints of one item (i.e. 3 in total), then p < (0.05/3) is needed?
By the way, shouldn't I also correct for the multiple chi-square tests that I perform to test for measurement invariance? (E.g., configural -> weak -> strong would be 2 tests). If so, does the P-value then need to be greater than P = (0.05*2)?

>
> > Lastly, I had thought that if the test would fail, that at least some intercepts (that I imposed to be equal over time) would pop up in the univariate tests. After all, that's the only thing that was changed between the weak and strong model. Where could I go from here to potentially show partial strong invariance?
>
> Well, the only 2 significant univariate tests are both associated with the intercept labeled .p57., although neither of them would be significant if you took steps to control your Type I error rate.  To perform fewer tests (and have more power), you could run only 1 post-hoc test of that item's intercepts:
>
> lavTestScore(fit, release = 18:20)
>
> If that particular 3-df post-hoc test is significant, release those constraints and compare the partial-strong model to the weak model using a LRT.
>

Shouldn't I also account for the first tests I did? That is, LavTestScore(fit) to identify which constraints needed to be released? Or how else should I know that I should release the intercepts associated with parameters 18:20, i.e. lavTestScore(fit, release = 18:20)?

Also, should I in general always release all or none of the intercepts associated with 1 item? Or does it make sense to only release some of its intercepts? Here, since parameter 18 and 20 were significant (univariate score tests), I would then test only to release those 2.

Either way the tests turns out insignificant: p = 0.09 for releasing 18:20 and p = 0.054 for releasing 18 and 20. But let's say it was significant and I would follow your advice and release the intercepts to test for partial measurement invariance afterwards. I'd think this latter test (chi-square test is what I would use), should also be corrected again, right?

Kind regards,
Amonet

I think the best advice depends on what you already know. If you know regression and factor analysis, then I like Loehlin's book (Latent Variable Models). Lots of people (including me) like Kline's book (Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling). There's also a Lavaan specific book (Latent Variable Modeling Using R).

Dan Bauer and Patrick Curran have  set of videos on Youtube about SEM: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC7kcXN1Xoj4PzMIKPHJ5m7Q/videos (There are probably others as well).

If you know multilevel models, have a look at the paper by Curran called "Have multilevel models been structural equation models all along".

If you come from a more mathematical background, there are probably better resources, but I don't know them. :)

Personally, I think that learning SEM on your own is hard - ideally, you should find a course to take, and you should make use of online resources (like this group) to ask questions and find answers.

Jeremy

messages.body_plain:
It's not necessarily a problem. You have high standard errors. These are correct - although it would be nice to be smaller, I don't think you should think of this as "a problem" to solve.

Increasing your sample size (all else being equal) will shrink your standard errors. (Quadruple your sample to halve your standard errors).

High standard errors also happen because of collinearity - your predictor variables are highly correlated. One solution is to remove a variable, another is to combine them (if they're highly correlated, they're tell your the same thing).

Terrence, thank you so much for all your help, i am sorry for all the questions.

> Q1) is the minimum test statistic being non-significant now suggest that the model fits better keeping the groups separated?

The test statistic for a model is testing whether that model fits as well as a saturated model (i.e., freely estimating all possible means and (co)variances).  It is not comparing that model to any other restricted/hypothesized model.

> Q3) how do i go about determining the df for that chi-square? my guess is # difference scores - 1...but i am not sure

The df for the test is listed with the test statistic. In order to test a particular hypothesis, you need to specify a model under which the null hypothesis is true (e.g., constrain differences to be equal, implying linearity) and a model under which the null is false (i.e., without the constraint), then compare those models using the anova() function, which returns a chi-squared difference test (along with its df).

Ah yes, that makes sense. My goal at this stage is to determine if the mean difference score at each time point is different between group 1 and group 2. So just to confirm that i have the logic right there are four possible versions of the constraints on the means (see below) and i would use the anova() command to compare between then (though the minimum test statistic would compare all of the models to free estimation). So my question is;

Q1) a significant minimum test statistic means that a given model is significantly different from free estimation of everything, which means that there is evidence that that constraint is not accurate (so if i constrained between the groups and it was significant then the groups should be different). messages.body_plain:
Hi Hervé,

A couple of comments to try to help
I don't think the measurementInvariance function is built to work with effects coding. The measurementInvariance function used the cfa command to fit all models, and to get effects coding to work you need to use the lavaan function (or override a lot of defaults on the cfa function)
Part of the reason the measurementInvariance function works this way is that the method of scale setting (fixed factor, marker variable, effects coding) does not affect model fit of a model or tests of differences between models. The method of scale setting only affects the parameter estimates. So the results you saw with the second run (using the defaults) are the same as what you would see with effects coding
There's an error in the effects coding syntax. For a multiple group model you need different labels (and different constraints) for each group. In addition, if you're working with effects coding you probably want to also specify constraints on the intercepts
Hope this helps,

Alex

messages.subject: CFA with categorical data and structured missingness
messages.subject_clean: CFA with categorical data and structured missingness
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
  I'm working on a set of confirmatory factor analyses of a set of items that have structured missingness. I know that this not ideal and it is relatively common among clinical measures.

The items are scored 0, 1, 2 as ordered categories. If you respond as a 2 on any of items 1-3, then items 4-10 administered. If you respond as a 0 or 1 on all of items 1-3, then items 4-10 are not administered. Approximately 30% of items 4-10 are missing. Conceptually the idea is that if you fail to pass the first 3 screening items, then you will not endorse any of the later items. In practice, I often see people just recoding these missing items as 0s. Recently, I've come across literature suggesting this is bad because it inflates the correlations among the items which could artificially reduce dimensionality in the factor structure.

I've fit the model a few different ways:
1) Code additional items as 0 with wlsmvs
cfa(model = mod.a, data = data, estimator = "WLSMVS", std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, verbose = TRUE, ordered = c("a1", "a2", "a3", "a4", "a5", "a6", "a7", "a8", "a9", "a10")
2) Leave additional items as missing and run wlsmvs with missing = "pairwise
cfa(model = mod.a, data = data, estimator = "WLSMVS", std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, verbose = TRUE, ordered = c("a1", "a2", "a3", "a4", "a5", "a6", "a7", "a8", "a9", "a10")
3) Treat it more like an IRT model (estimator = "MML")
cfa(model = mod.a, data = data, estimator = "MML", std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, verbose = TRUE, ordered = c("a1", "a2", "a3", "a4", "a5", "a6", "a7", "a8", "a9", "a10")

I've also considered doing multiple imputation of items 4-10 and then running WLSMVS on the imputed dataframes.

>From a results perspective,
1) Additional items as 0 with wlsmvs, gets cfi = .999, rmsea = .043, and very high factor loadings (lowest is > .7).
2) Additional items as missing with WLSMVS & missing = "pairwise", cfi = .977, rmsea = .06, and moderate factor loadings (.52 - .84).
3) estimator = "MML", no CFI/RMSEA provided, loadings rnge from .59 - 1.462 (I think these are actually discrimination parameters and not directly equivalent to a factor loading).

I haven't been able to find a clear answer on which approach is best. If anyone can provide feedback on which might be the best option (or if there is a best option that I haven't considered), help would be much appreciated.

Thank you,
Andrew

messages.subject: Re: Significance of R-Square in path model
messages.subject_clean: Significance of R-Square in path model
messages.body_plain:
Here's one way:

The significance of R-square is the joint significance of all of the parameters that predict a variable.

You can test the significance by fixing all of those parameters to be equal to zero. Here's a simple example that shows you get the same p-value in lavaan, and by using the lm() function:

library(lavaan)
set.seed(1234)
d <- data.frame(x1 = runif(1000), x2 = runif(1000))
d$y <- 0.05 * d$x1 + 0.05 * d$x2 + runif(1000)

summary(lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d))

mod1 <- "y ~ b1 * x1 + b2 * x2
         x1 ~~ x2
        "
fit1 <- sem(mod1, d)
summary(fit1)

mod0 <- "y ~ 0 * x1 + 0 * x2"
fit0 <- sem(mod0, d)
summary(fit0)

(If you're model is more complex, you might need to use anova() or you can do a Wald test with lavTestWald()).

Jeremy
