messages.subject: Re: Complex bifactor model: R won't run (crashes). help!
messages.subject_clean: Complex bifactor model: R won't run (crashes). help!
messages.body_plain:
Andy,
  First a caveat, then some thoughts.  The caveat:  I find it much easier to think through and debug complex models by started at zero and explicitly coding each aspect of the model using lavaan() with no convenience parameters than to start with part of the model specified by default and work backwards by removing parameters.  Perhaps that is just a matter of personal style.

  If I understand correctly, your model has 18 factors, 17 specific plus a general factor.  Your model specifies these as all being orthogonal to one another.

  The standard bifactor model allows the specific factors to covary and only requires that the general factor be orthogonal to the specific factors.

  Typically, items from different scales have non-zero correlations.  Oblique models account for such correlations without giving up simple structure by allowing the factors to correlate.  One can trace a path from and item on one scale, up to its factor, across a covariance to another factor, and down to an item on another scale.

  Orthogonal models do not allow the factors to covary and must therefore account for cross-scale correlations in another way.  Typically, this is done by giving up simple structure and allowing items to cross-load on factors for other scales.

  Your model is essentially an orthogonal model with a general factor added.  This general factor must alone account for all the correlations between items across scales.  With such a large number of diverse items, it may be unrealistic to expect a single dimension of covariation to entirely account for all the cross-scale correlations.

  I would first suggest that you reconsider whether you really meant the specific factors to be orthogonal.  If so, then I would start small, perhaps with two scales, and gradually build up the model until it starts to show problems.  Each time you add to the model, monitor what happens with the residuals.  This strategy may help you isolate the source of the problems.

  If none of that helps, I would suggest being more descriptive about exactly what happens when you try fit the model.  The term "crash" is vague and could refer to convergence to an improper solution, convergence failure, the lavaan function terminating early within R, or the R program itself closing on your computer.  Also, if you can reproduce the same behavior in a simple self-contained example that others can run, that may help facilitate an answer.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

Hi Terrence

I did what you suggested and i found some differences in the coefficients of the second stage, resulting in different predicted probabilities.

Here is what I do with lavaan

# create interaction of M and V

data$IA_MV<-data$M*data$V

model14<- ' # regressions
M~ 1+a1*X

Y ~ b1*M
Y ~ b2*V
Y ~ b3*IA_MV

Y ~ 1+cdash*X
'

# fit model

f.model14 <- sem(model = model14,
                  data = data,
                  se = "bootstrap",
                  bootstrap = 1000,

                 link = "probit")
These are the coefficient:
M~1=  6.526; a1=  -0.877; b1=   -0.962; b2= -0.094; b3= 0.014; cdash= 0.123; Y~1= 6.521

This is how i did it with the separate regression models:
M.model<-lm(M~X, data=data)
Y.model<-glm(Y~X+M+V+IA_MV,  data=data, family = binomial(link = "probit"))
These are the coefficients:

messages.subject: Re: SEM with second order latent variables
messages.subject_clean: SEM with second order latent variables
messages.body_plain:
In this case, I don't think it does.  The model is equivalent to a model that has arrows from the y1 and y2 to the two first order latent variables.

Here's how I think about it: If that latent variable wasn't there, you'd have four parameters - from the two Y vars to the two latents. When you add a latent variable you are specifying some constraints (usually) on what those four parameters might be. But when you add this latent, you still have four parameters - so you are not adding any constraints  - the two models are equivalent.

(Also, your Y variables are exogenous - it would be clearer if these were called X, and your X variables are endogenous. It would be clearer if these were called Y).

jeremy

I recommend that you rewrite the model a bit differently to simplify:

lv1 ~ x1 + x2 + lv2

lv2 =~ 0

x7 ~~ x11
x8 ~~ x9
x8 ~~ x10
x8 ~~ x11
x9 ~~ x10
x9 ~~ x11
x10 ~~ x11

Is that what you want to estimate?

The reason that the model is not identified is that in the regressions:

lv1 ~ x1 + x2 + lv2

lv2 ~ x3 + x4 + x5 + x6

The dependent variable does not have any observed consequences. This is the reason why many article recommend adding two effect (reflective) indicators to causal indicator models.

Mikko

H,

Yes. My mode was the same as yours, but presented in a simpler form. I assume that you want to define lv1 as a sum of x1 and x2, which you regress on lv2, but your model presented lv1 as a sum of x1, x2, and lv2. If you want to define a model where lv1 is defined as sum of x1 and x2, a lot simpler approach would be to just calculate that sum outside lavaan, drop the original variables, and use the sum instead in your model.

Doing this for both lv1 and lv2 will identify your model.

Alternatively, do you need lv1 and lv2? Why not just regress lv3 on x1-x6 and interpret those results. That would be identified as well.

Mikko

messages.body_plain:
Dear Keith et al.

Using

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,

              auto.cov.lv.x=F)

I believe that if you use non standardized coeficientes ([that is what you get with inspect(fit, "coef")$lambda],
your function should be

my.CR <- function(fit, ...){

  l<-inspect(fit,"coef")$lambda
  v<-diag(inspect(fit,"coef")$theta)

  ll <- colSums(l)^2*diag(inspect(fit,"coef")$psi)

  vm <- v %*% t(rep(1,length(ll)))
  sl <- sign(l^2)
  vv <- colSums(sl * vm)
  rr <- ll / (ll + vv)
  return(rr)
}

As you can see, I am changing
ll <- colSums(l)^2
to
ll <- colSums(l)^2*diag(inspect(fit,"coef")$psi)

Can you please confirm this?
Best,
João

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Non-convergence is a strong indication that your model is not identified. Consider that you scale L3 by constraining its variance to 1. The ovariance cov(x1, x7) is the product of regression of L3 on x1 and x7 on L3. In your model you have no empirical basis of how to split this covariance as the two paths that imply it. I use this scale setting approach because the underidentificatiin is easier to understand this way.

If you scale the latent variable by fixing the loading of x7 to 1, then the variance of L3 is not identified.

The reason for non-identification is that you free all the error covariance of x7-x10.

Mikko

messages.subject: Re: Composite reliability (CFA)
messages.subject_clean: Composite reliability (CFA)
messages.body_plain:
Joao & Jorge,
  Thanks for reviving this old thread and catching the inconsistency between the model specification and the omega calculation.  Jorge and I exchanged email about the thread off list yesterday.  For clarity, I decided to post three analyses of data provided as a worked example by Rod McDonald in his 1999 Test Theory book.

# McDonald1999, Table 6.3, Page 82
McDonald1999 <- c(2.5666, 1.560, 1.487, 1.195, 1.425, 1.560, 2.493, 1.283, 0.845, 1.313, 1.487, 1.283, 2.462, 1.127, 1.313, 1.195, 0.845, 1.127, 2.769, 1.323, 1.425, 1.313, 1.313, 1.323, 3.356)
McDonald1999Cov <- matrix(data=McDonald1999, ncol=5, nrow=5)
McDonald1999Names <- paste0('item', 1:5)
dimnames(McDonald1999Cov) <- list(McDonald1999Names, McDonald1999Names)
McDonald1999Cov

# Unit loading
McDonaldModelLoading <- '
  LV =~ 1*item1 + item2 + item3 + item4 + item5
  LV ~~ LV
  item1 ~~ item1
  item2 ~~ item2
  item3 ~~ item3
  item4 ~~ item4
  item5 ~~ item5
' # end model

# Unit variance
McDonaldModelVariance <- '
  LV =~ item1 + item2 + item3 + item4 + item5
  LV ~~ 1*LV
  item1 ~~ item1
  item2 ~~ item2
  item3 ~~ item3
  item4 ~~ item4
  item5 ~~ item5
' # end model

# Fit models
fitUnitLoading <- lavaan(model=McDonaldModelLoading, sample.cov=McDonald1999Cov, sample.nobs=215, estimator='ULS')
fitUnitVariance <- lavaan(model=McDonaldModelVariance, sample.cov=McDonald1999Cov, sample.nobs=215, estimator='ULS')

# Extract estimates
c1<-lavInspect(fitUnitLoading,"coef")
l1<-c1$lambda
v1<-diag(c1$theta)
p1<-c1$psi[1,1]

c2<-lavInspect(fitUnitVariance,"coef")
l2<-c2$lambda
v2<-diag(c2$theta)
p2<-c2$psi[1,1]

c3<-lavInspect(fitUnitLoading,"std")
l3<-c3$lambda
v3<-diag(c3$theta)
p3<-c3$psi[1,1]

# Visually inspect estimates
l1;l2;l3
v1;v2;v3
p1;p2;p3

# Compute omega
omega1 <- ((sum(l1)^2)*p1) / (((sum(l1)^2)*p1) + sum(v1))
omega2 <- (sum(l2)^2) / ((sum(l2)^2) + sum(v2))
omega3 <- (sum(l3)^2) / ((sum(l3)^2) + sum(v3)) # not appropriate

# McDonald 1999 page 90 calculates .8189 or .8188
omega1; omega2; omega3

omega1b <- ((sum(l2)^2)*p2) / (((sum(l2)^2)*p2) + sum(v2))
omega1b

The estimates are as follows.  Note that I used ULS estimation to match the worked example.

> omega1; omega2; omega3
[1] 0.8189322
[1] 0.8189322
[1] 0.8222746

The take away:
1. Method 1 (multiplying by the factor variance) is a general method that will work for either a unit loading or a unit factor variance.

2. Method 2 (no such multiplication) assumes that unit factor variance but will return the same result when that assumption is correct.

3. Method 3 uses standardized loading and is not appropriate as an estimate of raw omega because the raw total score effectively weights the items by their variances whereas the standardized solution gives them equal weights.  This method instead estimates the total score derived from converting the items to z scores before computing the total score.  This is analogous to standardized alpha.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Factor loadings of indicators on a group factor switches when applied a bi-factor model
messages.subject_clean: Factor loadings of indicators on a group factor switches when applied a bi-factor model
messages.body_plain:
Hello.  I am trying to apply bi-factor model to a 3 factor model (each factor has 4 indicators).

When I apply a bi-factor model, two of indicators on a single factor show negative factor loadings, although they were originally positive.  I am wondering if it is acceptable to constrain factor loadings of these indicators to positive (e.g., 0.1)?

My bi-factor model is:

library(lavaan)

ABC.model <- 'A =~ NA*A1 + A2 + A3 + A4

B =~ NA*B1 + B2 + B3 + B4

C =~ NA*C1 + C2 + C3 + C4

G =~ NA*A1 + A2 + A3 + A4 + B1 + B2 + B3 + B4 + C1 + C2 + C3 + C4'

 fit <- cfa(ABC.model, data=Data, estimator="WLSMV", orthogonal=TRUE, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)

Thank you very much for your help!

J

messages.subject: Weight least square fitting function for multilevel ordinal CFA
messages.subject_clean: Weight least square fitting function for multilevel ordinal CFA
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to get a solid understanding of how a multilevel ordinal CFA gets fit to the sample data. My question is, what does the WLS fitting function look like for this multilevel scheme used in lavaan? I couldn't find any article elaborating on this issue with respect to ordinal data but of course I am there must be a few out there.

My speculation is that polychoric correlation matrix is estimated for each cluster. Subsequently, WLS fitting function for each cluster can be constructed. The goal is to minimize the sum of fitting functions derived from all clusters. Is my speculation correct? Thank you very much.

Best,
Chao
